You now have two verb-factories: -thirri (become, Lesson 21) and -marama (make/cause, Lesson 20). There's a third machine in the workshop, and it completes the set: -kuma / -guma / -yama, which takes an ADJECTIVE and forges a transitive verb: to make something be that quality.

marŋgi (knowing) → marŋgikuma → to make-knowing → to teach

Sit with that etymology. Teaching, in this language, is literally to cause someone to know. Not to transmit information. Not to lecture. To make-knowing. The learner is the object being transformed, and the teacher is the agent of that transformation. (Hebrew speakers: this is your causative binyan again, לימד from ידע. Same machine, other side of the planet.)

Ŋarra balaŋu marŋgikuŋu ŋanya → I should teach him

And now watch all three factories line up around a single quality:

marŋgi → knowing (the state)
marŋgithirri → to come to know, to learn (become it)
marŋgikuma → to teach (make someone else it)

One root. The state, the becoming, the causing. That triangle exists for quality after quality: manymak (good) can be become-good or be made-good; muk (quiet) gives mukthirri-style becoming and mukmarama making-quiet from Lesson 20. Check the dictionary for which factory each root prefers, some take -kuma, some -marama, some both.

And here's the bigger realisation this unlocks, one that quietly rewires how you translate: many English adjectives are simply verbs in Gupapuyŋu. You've already been doing it:

They are happy → Walala djulŋithina (they happied, they became-happy)
I'm tired → Ŋarra djawaryurruna (I tired)
He got sick → Ŋayi rerrimirrithina

English freezes these states into adjectives and props them up with to be. Gupapuyŋu lets them stay verbs, alive, with tense, with becoming built in. So stop hunting for a missing is when you translate. Ask instead: is this state secretly an event? Here, it usually is.

States, becomings, causings, all one family, all built with suffixes you can hold in one hand. The workshop is small. The language it builds is not.
